## Example 8.6 {#ss8-example-8-6 .growth-lesson .growth-dense .growth-salary}

<div class="eyebrow">2013 Advanced HSC 12c · 7 marks</div>

Kim and Alex start jobs at the beginning of the same year. Kim’s annual salary in the first year is **\$30 000** and increases by **5%** at the beginning of each subsequent year. Alex’s annual salary in the first year is **\$33 000**, and increases by **\$1500** at the beginning of each subsequent year.

<div class="growth-subparts">

**(a)** Show that in the 10th year, Kim’s annual salary is higher than Alex’s annual salary. <span class="growth-marks">(2 marks)</span>

**(b)** In the first 10 years how much, in total, does Kim earn? <span class="growth-marks">(2 marks)</span>

**(c)** Every year, Alex saves $\dfrac13$ of her annual salary. How many years does it take her to save \$87 500? <span class="growth-marks">(3 marks)</span>

</div>

<p class="booklet-cue">Booklet p. 53 · Example 8.6</p>

::: notes

Complete working in OneNote. Kim’s salaries form a GP; Alex’s form an AP. The first stated salary is Year 1, so the tenth salary follows nine increases. (a) K_10=30000(1.05)^9=$46539.84647935549≈$46539.85. A_10=33000+9(1500)=$46500, so Kim earns about $39.85 more. (b) Kim’s total=30000(1.05^10−1)/(1.05−1)=$377336.7760664651≈$377336.78. (c) Alex’s cumulative savings=(1/3)(n/2)[2(33000)+(n−1)1500]=250n²+10750n. Equate to 87500: n²+43n−350=0=(n−7)(n+50). Accept n=7 years; n=−50 is not meaningful. Savings after 6 years are $73500 and after 7 are $87500. The 1/3 multiplies the whole arithmetic sum. Preserve the HSC attribution and mark allocation supplied in the booklet.

:::
